name: Schwarzschild-Tangherlini Black Hole
description: The Schwarzschild black hole in $D \ge 4$ spacetime dimensions, the static vacuum solution with hyperspherical symmetry that Frank Tangherlini found in 1963. Its metric function is $1 - (r_h/r)^{D-3}$, and for $D > 4$ every circular orbit of a massive particle around it is unstable.
convention: The horizon radius $r_h$ is fixed by the mass $M$ through $r_h^{D-3} = 16\pi GM/\left((D-2)\,\Omega_{D-2}\,c^2\right)$, with $G$ Newton's constant in $D$ spacetime dimensions and $\Omega_{D-2}$ the area of the unit sphere of $D - 2$ dimensions. We keep factors of $c$ explicit.
history: Paul Ehrenfest asked in 1917 how the fundamental laws of physics show that space has three dimensions [ehrenfest1917]. In a space of $n$ dimensions Newton's force of gravity falls as $1/r^{n-1}$, and Ehrenfest found that for $n > 3$ a planet disturbed from a circular orbit "falls on the attracting centre or flies away infinitely" [ehrenfest1917]. Gerald Whitrow reached the same result independently in 1955 [whitrow1955, tangherlini1963].¶Frank Tangherlini put the question to general relativity in 1963 [tangherlini1963]. He generalised Karl Schwarzschild's field of 1916 to a static mass with hyperspherical symmetry in $n$ space dimensions [tangherlini1963, schwarzschild1916]. In $D = n + 1$ spacetime dimensions his metric function is $$f(r) = 1 - \frac{\mu}{r^{D-3}},$$ Schwarzschild's $1 - r_s/r$ with the fall of the Newtonian potential in $D$ dimensions in place of $1/r$, and it solves the vacuum field equations [emparan2008]. Tangherlini postulated that "there shall be stable bound orbits" for the equations of motion of interacting bodies, and showed from the geodesics of his field that the postulate holds only for $n = 3$ [tangherlini1963]. For the Schrödinger hydrogen atom in $n$ dimensions he found that the same postulate excludes $n > 3$ [tangherlini1963].¶Vitor Cardoso, Alex Miranda, Emanuele Berti, Helvi Witek and Vilson Zanchin worked out the circular geodesics of the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini metric in 2009 [cardoso2009]. For $D > 4$ every circular orbit of a massive particle is unstable, and in four dimensions the circular orbits are stable at every radius beyond $3r_s$ [cardoso2009]. Light circles the black hole at $r = \left(\tfrac{D-1}{2}\right)^{1/(D-3)}r_h$, where $r_h$ is the radius of the horizon, and that orbit is unstable for every $D \ge 4$ [cardoso2009]. They showed that the equatorial circular orbits of massive particles around a rotating black hole are unstable as well for $D \ge 5$ [cardoso2009].¶Robert Myers and Malcolm Perry studied the static black holes of $D$ dimensions in 1986 and found the family of spinning ones [myers1986]. The horizon of the static black hole is the sphere $r_h = \mu^{1/(D-3)}$, and its mass $M$ fixes $\mu = 16\pi GM/\left((D-2)\,\Omega_{D-2}\,c^2\right)$, with $\Omega_{D-2}$ the area of the unit sphere of $D - 2$ dimensions [emparan2008]. A black hole of $D$ dimensions can rotate in several independent planes at once [emparan2008]. For $D \ge 6$ Myers and Perry found that a black hole of fixed mass may have arbitrarily large angular momentum [myers1986]. Roberto Emparan and Harvey Reall found a rotating black ring in five dimensions in 2002, a vacuum solution whose horizon has the topology $S^1 \times S^2$ [emparan2002]. For a range of mass and angular momentum two black rings and a Myers-Perry black hole exist with the same values of both, so the uniqueness theorems of four dimensions "do not have simple higher dimensional generalizations" [emparan2002].¶Ruth Gregory and Raymond Laflamme found in 1993 that a black string, a black hole extended along one more flat direction, is unstable to perturbations of long wavelength along that direction [gregorylaflamme1993, emparan2008]. Gary Gibbons, Daisuke Ida and Tetsuya Shiromizu proved in 2002 that the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini solution is the only static, asymptotically flat vacuum black hole for $D > 4$ [gibbons2002, emparan2008]. Hideo Kodama and Akihiro Ishibashi reduced the gravitational perturbations of such a black hole in 2003 to a single wave equation for one master variable [kodama2003]. Ishibashi and Kodama used it the same year to show that the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini black hole is stable against linear perturbations [ishibashi2003].¶Nima Arkani-Hamed, Savas Dimopoulos and Gia Dvali proposed in 1998 that space has two or more compact dimensions large compared to the weak scale, with gravity becoming strong at energies near a TeV [arkanihamed1998]. Philip Argyres, Dimopoulos and John March-Russell showed the same year that a black hole smaller than those dimensions is "bigger, colder, and longer-lived than a usual $(3+1)$-dimensional black hole of the same mass" [argyres1998]. Steven Giddings and Scott Thomas, and Dimopoulos and Greg Landsberg, calculated in 2001 that with the scale of quantum gravity near a TeV the Large Hadron Collider would produce such black holes, at a rate Dimopoulos and Landsberg put at about one every second [giddings2002, dimopoulos2001]. The CMS collaboration searched 35 pb$^{-1}$ of proton collisions at 7 TeV for their decays in 2011 and found agreement with the standard model backgrounds [cms2011]. Its limits on the minimum black hole mass, between 3.5 and 4.5 TeV, were "the first direct limits on black hole production at a particle accelerator" [cms2011]. Emparan, Ryotaku Suzuki and Kentaro Tanabe took the limit $D \to \infty$ in 2013, where the dynamics of a black hole occurs at lengths $1/D$ times smaller than its horizon radius [emparan2013].

related.text: The case $D = 4$, where the metric function is $1 - r_s/r$ and a massive particle has stable circular orbits.
A second static vacuum solution of gravity in five dimensions. It has no horizon, and its 3-spheres are squashed and close smoothly at the centre [grossperry1983].

Schwarzschild's black hole stretched along a line, the other black hole of five dimensions. A long enough piece of it has less entropy than Tangherlini's round hole of the same mass, and it is unstable [gregorylaflamme1993].
Tangherlini's black hole set spinning, in as many planes as its dimension has room for. With every spin at zero it is his metric again [myers1986].
The spinning black hole of four dimensions. Robert Myers and Malcolm Perry found its counterparts in $D$ dimensions in 1986, with the static black hole as the member that does not turn [myers1986].

Tangherlini's black hole of five dimensions with the curvature squared term of string theory added to the action. The term brings a length $\ell$ with it, and at $\ell = 0$ the metric is Tangherlini's [boulware1985].

A black ring in balance around a spinning hole. With the two turning against each other it can match Tangherlini's hole in mass and in having no angular momentum, so in five dimensions those two numbers do not fix the black hole [elvang2007].
Tangherlini's hole of five dimensions given three charges. Each charge rescales its time and its space by a power of a harmonic function of its own [horowitz1996].

A star with no horizon built from Tangherlini's black hole: give it a circle, exchange the circle with time, and hold the resulting bubble open with flux. With four large dimensions it is the topological star of five [bah2021].

coordinates.name: Hyperspherical, Five Dimensions

parameters.description: Horizon radius, $r_h^{D-3} = 16\pi GM/\left((D-2)\,\Omega_{D-2}\,c^2\right)$ in $D$ spacetime dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 5$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r_h^2 = 8GM/(3\pi c^2)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein, Five Dimensions

parameters.description: Horizon radius, $r_h^{D-3} = 16\pi GM/\left((D-2)\,\Omega_{D-2}\,c^2\right)$ in $D$ spacetime dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 5$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r - \tfrac{1}{2}r_h\ln\left|\dfrac{r - r_h}{r + r_h}\right|$ a length.

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein, Five Dimensions

parameters.description: Horizon radius, $r_h^{D-3} = 16\pi GM/\left((D-2)\,\Omega_{D-2}\,c^2\right)$ in $D$ spacetime dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 5$, with the advanced time $v = ct + r + \tfrac{1}{2}r_h\ln\left|\dfrac{r - r_h}{r + r_h}\right|$ a length.

coordinates.name: Hyperspherical, Six Dimensions

parameters.description: Horizon radius, $r_h^{D-3} = 16\pi GM/\left((D-2)\,\Omega_{D-2}\,c^2\right)$ in $D$ spacetime dimensions

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \chi, \psi, \theta, \phi)$ in $D = 6$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r_h^3 = 3GM/(2\pi c^2)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
